Product & experience

One application. Three platforms. A beginner mixes two tracks in seconds; an experienced DJ plays a full set without feeling constrained.

1. Challenging the brief

Assumption in the briefProblemWhat we do instead
Four separate levels (Quick Control → Mix → DJ Mode → Pro Studio)Mode switches hide state ("where did my EQ go?") and make users choose an identity up frontOne workspace with progressive density. The same session, decks and mixer exist at every level; density reveals more of them. A beginner's EQ move is still there when they expand the view
A phone can cue privately with the right softwareOn iPhone it can't without hardware (see research); on Android it depends on the modelSay so in plain language at setup, recommend the cheapest fix (splitter cable), and make the no-cue experience genuinely good: visual beat-matching, auto-sync, and phrase-aware automatic transitions so cueing by ear is optional
Beginners need simple EQBeginners don't know when to use EQTransitions apply DJ technique for them (bass swap, filter sweep, echo out) on the phrase, and show what they did so it can be learned
BPM detection is enoughTracks have different loudness, keys and phrase structureAuto-gain to −10 LUFS, key detection with Camelot compatibility, phrase-aligned transitions, "what plays well next" suggestions
Streaming musicDRM catalogues need licensed partner integrations; Spotify is desktop-only for DJ appsLocal files first; provider-pluggable library; partnerships are a business workstream from day one
Bluetooth is just another output100–200 ms makes cueing impossible and makes visuals lieAccept it for master, compensate visuals and the cue bus, never for cueing
Recording is a featureRecording what the master sounded like is a correctness feature (post-limiter tap, never drops)Lock-free record tap; set history with timestamps for tracklists

2. Missing capabilities worth building

  1. Phrase detection (8/16/32-bar boundaries) — transitions start on phrases, not just beats.
  2. Next-track suggestions — tempo range, Camelot neighbours, energy, history.
  3. Key-lock / master tempo — tempo changes without pitch change (time-stretch).
  4. Slip mode, beat-quantised hot cues and loops, censor/reverse — expected by experienced DJs.
  5. Stems (vocals/drums/bass/other) — on-device separation; acapella-in, instrumental-out.
  6. Ableton Link — tempo sync with other apps and devices in the room.
  7. MIDI/HID controller mapping with a shared mapping format across platforms; class-compliant first.
  8. Set history & tracklist export — for radio/streaming compliance and for learning.
  9. Crash-safe performance — the engine keeps playing if the UI stalls; the session restores mid-set.
  10. Thermal/battery awareness — reduce waveform frame rate and analysis concurrency during a set.
  11. Interruption policy — phone calls/notifications during a set: Do-Not-Disturb prompt, audio session interruption handling, resume without jumps.
  12. Practice mode — the app plays the "other DJ": it sets up the next track and the learner performs the transition, with feedback.

3. The progressive workspace

Density is a continuous property of one layout, chosen automatically from screen size and manually by the user (pinch on the workspace, ⌘+/⌘− on Mac).

Level 1 — Quick Control (phone portrait, default for new users)

  • One large Now Playing waveform (scrolling, three-band colour), artwork-free by design.
  • Up Next card: suggested track with BPM/key compatibility badges.
  • One primary action: Mix (picks transition style and length; starts on the next phrase).
  • Master volume, a single Bass / Mid / Treble row, one Filter knob for the playing track.
  • Output chip at the top: "Speaker · no headphone cue" / "Headphones cue ready" — tapping it explains.

Level 2 — Mix (phone landscape, tablets)

  • Two decks stacked: parallel waveforms with aligned beat grids (the fastest way to see sync).
  • Crossfader, per-deck play/cue/sync, tempo, BPM/key, cue-points strip.
  • Library sheet with preview-in-headphones (hold a row to preview; release to stop).
  • Transition picker (Blend · Bass swap · Filter · Echo out, 4/8/16/32 beats).

Level 3 — DJ Mode (tablet, Mac, phone landscape at high density)

  • Full mixer: trim, 3-band EQ with kill, filter, channel fader, PFL, cue/master blend, headphone level.
  • 8 performance pads per deck: hot cues · loops · beat jump · rolls.
  • Recording, set history, quantise, key-lock, slip.

Level 4 — Pro Studio (Mac, iPad with keyboard, Android tablets/desktop mode)

  • Up to 4 decks, routing matrix (bus → device channel), latency calibration, MIDI learn, saved layouts per controller, sampler, external input decks.

4. Design language

Decided: Obsidian is the default design system, and users can restyle it in Settings › Appearance (theme, accent, deck view including Radial, waveform colours, density). See design/appearance.md and design/tokens/obsidian.tokens.json.

  • Original, not skeuomorphic. No fake jog wheels or brushed metal. Controls are typographic and geometric; the waveform is the hero.
  • Colour has meaning, never alone. Deck A cool, deck B warm, consistently across waveform, pads and crossfader; every colour cue also has a label, position or shape.
  • Three-band waveform: low = deep saturated, mid = neutral, high = bright; amplitude from the engine's waveform bins; beat grid as hairlines, downbeats heavier, phrase starts marked.
  • Type: one variable sans for UI, tabular numerals for BPM/time; large numerals for the two numbers DJs glance at — BPM and time remaining.
  • Motion communicates timing: beat-pulse on the sync button, phrase countdown before an automatic transition, no decorative animation. Reduce Motion respected.
  • Touch: big targets (≥ 44 pt), hold-to-preview, drag on waveform to nudge (rate bend, not seek), two-finger drag to scrub, pinch to zoom, haptic tick on beats while nudging.
  • Desktop: full keyboard map (space = play A, ⇧space = play B, Q/W cue, 1–8 hot cues, ←/→ beat jump), pointer hover reveals fine controls, every control MIDI-learnable.
  • Accessibility: VoiceOver/TalkBack labels with values ("Deck B tempo plus 1.6 percent, synced"), Dynamic Type for non-performance chrome, high-contrast waveform theme, haptic beat for low-vision beat-matching.

5. The two-tracks-in-seconds flow

  1. Open the app → last session restored or Pick a track (local files).
  2. It plays. Up Next suggests a compatible track (already analysed in the background).
  3. Tap Mix. The app syncs the next track, aligns it to the phrase, counts down, and performs a bass-swap blend over 16 beats.
  4. A one-line note explains what happened ("Swapped the basslines at the half-way point") — learning by doing.

Measured target: from launch with a library to a completed transition in under 30 seconds, no hardware, no settings.
